chunks: Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man with whom I had kinship ties who died, leaving behind young children, and leaving behind his slaves, boys and girls, and he did not make a will. What do you think regarding the one who buys from them a female slave and takes her as an Umm Walad (mother of a child), and what do you think regarding their sale? He said: 'If they have a guardian who manages their affairs, sells on their behalf, and looks after their interests, he is rewarded in doing so.' I said: 'What do you think regarding the one who buys from them a female slave and takes her as an Umm Walad?' He said: 'There is no harm in that, if the guardian for them, the one who looks after what benefits them, sells on their behalf, and they have no right to return (revoke) what the guardian for them and the one who looks after what benefits them has done.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on selling slave children by their guardian in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the fiduciary authority of a guardian (wali) over the property of minor orphans, specifically regarding the sale of slave girls. The ruling establishes that if the guardian acts in the orphans' best interest by selling a female slave who subsequently becomes an *Umm Walad* (mother of a child), the transaction is binding and irrevocable, highlighting the practical application of estate management in early Shia jurisprudence.
